items.prompt: Before the fix, PATCH /api/tasks/[id] already ran updateMany with where { id, userId }. Why did Alice still manage to move her task into Bob's project?
items.answer: The where clause protects the source task row only; nothing checked who owned the destination project written via data: body
distractors: updateMany ignores the where clause when the data contains a foreign key
Prisma's updateMany bypasses foreign key constraints in SQLite
The userId filter was applied after the write instead of before it
items.explanation: Authorization must cover every resource whose relationship the operation changes, not just the row being updated.

items.prompt: The destination lookup returns the same 404 'Project not found' whether the project does not exist or belongs to another user. Why not a 403 for the second case?
items.answer: A distinct answer would be an id oracle, telling the caller that someone else's project with that id exists
distractors: Next.js route handlers cannot return a 403 status
A 403 would make the client retry the request with a refreshed session
Prisma's findFirst cannot distinguish the two cases, so the route has no choice
items.explanation: Combining id and userId in one predicate makes absent and out-of-scope indistinguishable by design.

items.prompt: Why does the PATCH guard test body.projectId !== undefined instead of if (body.projectId)?
items.answer: An empty string parses under z.string().optional() and would still reach updateMany via data: body, but a truthiness check would skip the lookup for it
distractors: Because the schema turns an omitted projectId into null, which is truthy-safe
Because TypeScript forbids truthiness checks on optional string fields
Because an undefined projectId means 'remove the task from its project'
items.explanation: Presence, not truthiness, decides whether the relationship changes. Authorization should never depend on favorable coercion.

items.prompt: Alice PATCHes her own task with only { title: 'New title' }. What does the route do?
items.answer: Skips the project lookup, runs updateMany scoped to { id, userId }, re-reads the task and returns it with 200
distractors: Looks up the task's current project to confirm ownership, then updates
Returns 400 because projectId is required on every task write
Returns 404 because no project id was supplied to validate
items.explanation: Omission means the request does not change the relationship, so no destination needs authorizing.

items.prompt: Where exactly does the POST /api/tasks ownership lookup run, and why does it select only id?
items.answer: After taskSchema.parse and before task.create; the decision needs existence-within-scope, not the project object
distractors: Before parsing, so malformed bodies are rejected by the lookup
After task.create, so the new task id can be included in the check
Inside a transaction with the create, which requires selecting all columns
items.explanation: The guard sits between validation and the write; everything else in the create path (defaults, 201) is unchanged.

items.prompt: Why does the regression record every create/updateMany call and its arguments rather than only asserting a 404 status?
items.answer: A handler that wrote first and then returned 404 would show the same status while still creating the forbidden relationship
distractors: Status codes are unreliable in Next.js route handler tests
Recording calls is needed to measure the guard's performance overhead
The 404 body text changes between Prisma versions
items.explanation: The negative assertion that matters is that the forbidden relationship produces no task write.

items.prompt: You delete the POST guard at tasks/route.ts lines 38-44. The 'creates with the owned project' test still passes. What does that teach?
items.answer: A positive case alone cannot detect a missing guard and a negative case alone cannot detect a guard that rejects everything - you need both
distractors: The owned-project test is redundant and should be deleted
The guard was dead code, since the create would have failed anyway
Tests that check only status codes are always sufficient for authorization
items.explanation: Only 'rejects a foreign project before create' fails, because it checks that no project read led to a create.

items.prompt: A POST /api/tasks body omits projectId entirely. What happens?
items.answer: taskSchema requires projectId, so parsing throws a ZodError and the route returns 400 without any lookup
distractors: The task is created without a project and the lookup is skipped
The lookup runs with id undefined and the route returns 404
The route assigns the user's default project and returns 201
items.explanation: Unlike PATCH, POST's taskSchema declares projectId: z.string() with no optional, so omission is a validation failure.

items.prompt: POST /api/projects with a nonexistent areaId returns a 400 with a Prisma foreign-key message; with Bob's real areaId it returns 201. Why is that a problem?
items.answer: handleError echoes error.message for any Error, so the difference reveals whether an id exists and leaks internals
distractors: Prisma messages are localized and break non-English clients
A 400 for a missing foreign key violates the HTTP specification
It is not a problem, because cuid ids cannot be guessed
items.explanation: The fix is an ownership lookup returning the same 404 for both cases plus a generic message for non-validation errors.

items.prompt: Settings import creates each row as { ...item, userId }. What can a caller still control?
items.answer: Every column except userId - including id and foreign keys like projectId or areaId - because there is no schema on the rows
distractors: Nothing; spreading userId last discards every caller-supplied field
Only userId, because it is the last property written
Only display fields such as names, since ids are regenerated by Prisma
items.explanation: Spreading userId last stops forging ownership, but the caller still chooses ids and relationships: mass assignment.

items.prompt: Alice deletes her project between her own task POST's lookup and its task.create. What does the client see?
items.answer: The Task_projectId_fkey constraint rejects the insert and handleError returns a 400 carrying the raw Prisma message - ugly, but no cross-user relationship
distractors: A task pointing at a deleted project is created and orphaned
A clean 404 'Project not found', because the guard re-checks after create
A deadlock, because the delete and the create lock the same row
items.explanation: Lookup and write are two statements; the database's foreign key preserves integrity, and only the response is untidy.

items.prompt: Why doesn't the lookup-then-write gap let a project change owner between Alice's check and her write?
items.answer: No API path writes Project.userId: the project PATCH schema allows only areaId, name and order, and settings import forces userId to the caller
distractors: Because the lookup and write share one Prisma transaction
Because SQLite serializes all writes, so no interleaving is possible
Because project ids are cuids and cannot be guessed by another user
items.explanation: Choose the mechanism from an actual invariant and failure scenario: only an ownership-transfer feature would require a composite FK or conditional insert.

items.front: Reviewer says 'PATCH already filters by userId, so the project check is redundant' (src/app/api/tasks/[id]/route.ts:23-36). Give the counterexample.
items.back: Alice owns task A; Bob owns project B. Alice PATCHes A with projectId B. updateMany({ where: { id: A, userId: Alice } }) matches, so without the guard A points into Bob's project. The project query needs { id: B, userId: Alice }, the task write needs { id: A, userId: Alice }: neither predicate replaces the other.

items.front: The worked change fixed tasks only. Name the bug class still open in POST /api/daytask (src/app/api/daytask/route.ts:33-42) and its siblings.
items.back: Unchecked relationship ids: body.taskId (and goalId, areaId elsewhere) is written without looking the target up with the caller's userId. Once a DayTask points at Bob's task, GET /api/day's includes turn the write into a read leak of Bob's task, project and area names.

items.front: Write the shape of the destination ownership guard used in POST /api/tasks (src/app/api/tasks/route.ts:38-44).
items.back: findFirst({ where: { id: body.projectId, userId: auth.user.id }, select: { id: true } }); if nothing comes back, return 404 'Project not found' before any write. One predicate pair proves the relationship is allowed at that moment.

items.front: What does handleError (src/lib/api.ts:13-29) return for a ZodError, for any other Error, and for a non-Error throw?
items.back: ZodError: 400 'Validation failed' with the issues. Any other Error: 400 with error.message verbatim - which is how raw Prisma constraint messages leak to clients. Anything else: 500 'Unknown error'.
